text: Everything ITIL 4 teaches sits inside one container: the Service Value System. It describes how all of an organization's components and activities work together to enable value creation, for the organization and for its customers. It takes in opportunity and demand — a new idea, a customer request, a regulatory requirement, anything that could prompt the organization to act — and converts it into value.

That conversion happens through five interacting components: Guiding Principles, Governance, the Service Value Chain, Practices, and Continual Improvement. No single component does the whole job. They operate together, which is exactly why ITIL 4 dropped the rigid, sequential lifecycle from version three.

Guiding Principles are seven recommendations — things like focus on value, and start where you are — that guide decision-making in any circumstance, regardless of which practice is in play. They're deliberately few and general, so they apply everywhere. Governance is the means by which the organization is directed and controlled, setting the boundaries everything else operates inside.

The Service Value Chain is the operational core: six interconnected activities — plan, improve, engage, design and transition, obtain or build, and deliver and support — that convert demand into value. It's deliberately not a fixed sequence. Those activities draw on the thirty-four practices to actually get work done.

Continual Improvement is both one specific practice and a thread running through every other component. Governance, the value chain, and every practice are all expected to keep improving — it isn't a phase that happens once at the end.

That's the real shift from ITIL v3: instead of a lifecycle you move through stage by stage, the Service Value System is one system you operate continuously, all its parts active at once. Chapters 2 and 3 go deep on the Guiding Principles and the Value Chain. Up next: Chapter 2, starting with Focus on Value.
